clue.text: Were attractive buttocks one result of playing 9 25?

parts.note: a thing that caught the eye or the fancy was attractive, so caught can stand for were attractive
behind is an informal word for the buttocks

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether a pair of shapely buttocks came from playing some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 25 is IN THE CORRIDOR OF UNCERTAINTY, cricket's name for the line just outside off stump, where a batter unsure whether to play edges it to the wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a batter who edges the ball to the wicketkeeper is out in this way, a typical dismissal from such deliveries.

clue.text: Observer's angle reported as 'a bit much … lacking basics of language, sadly'

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: the clue word as, said aloud, sounds like the letters A Z

indicators.note: sadly means in a sorry state, so the remaining letters are jumbled
lacking means without, so these letters are removed

parts.note: the ABC is the basics of anything, as of language

explanation.surface: Someone's viewpoint is described as excessive and linguistically crude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' makes 'as' sound like AZ; 'lacking' removes A, B and C from ABITMUCH, leaving ITMUH, which 'sadly' shuffles to IMUTH.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy and navigation this is the bearing measured round the horizon from north, the angle an observer sights along.

clue.text: As corrupted witness implied?

definitions.meaning: a witness who has been bribed or intimidated has been ...
what someone ... is what they hinted or implied

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are idioms: tampering with someone means getting at them, and getting at a point means suggesting it.

clue.text: Perennial chart-topper, not always poetical, opening up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: the record at the top of the chart is No 1, written NO I

indicators.note: the word not is opened up to let the poet's word in

parts.note: e'er is the poetic form of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A hit record that stays popular year after year, though not always in a poetic way, starts to open up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perennial' looks like it describes the chart-topper; it is a garden plant. The whole wordplay is read upwards, bottom to top, as fits a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: This onion grows small bulbs at the top of its stem and comes back every year, so it is a perennial.

clue.text: Novel by Shaw and older books bound to get a place, at least

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are bound round the books, holding them inside
novel means new or unusual, so the letters of these words are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: OT, the Old Testament, holds the older books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A book-collector hopes a novel by Shaw plus some old volumes will win at least a place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book; it signals the anagram. 'to get' links. A bet laid this way, each way, pays out if the horse wins or is placed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bet laid this way pays on a win or a place, so it covers coming in the frame at the very least.

clue.text: Merseyside town's good deal on the black market?

parts.note: Bootle is a town in Merseyside, just north of Liverpool

explanation.surface: A Liverpool-area town has a good deal on the black market.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOTLE is a town in Merseyside, the county around Liverpool. The question mark marks the definition as a verb used loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: To bootleg is to make or sell goods illicitly, originally smuggled liquor, which is trading on the black market.

clue.text: In what's upsetting to Arab hearts repeatedly skipping a beat

indicators.note: in places the next piece inside the shuffled letters
upsetting means knocking over, so these letters are rearranged
skipping means leaving out, so these letters are removed
repeatedly means the single letter is taken twice over

parts.note: H is the card abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: Something upsetting to an Arab makes his heart miss beats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skipping' removes two As ('a', 'repeatedly') from TOARAB, giving TORB; 'upsetting' shuffles it, and 'In' sets H inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a strong pulse or beat, as of a heart.

clue.text: With IDs falsified, Telegraph employees 1 Across!

indicators.note: falsified means faked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the Telegraph's own staff would say we of themselves

explanation.surface: Newspaper staff use fake identity papers.
explanation.walkthrough: '1' points the reader to 1 Across, but only 'Across' defines: the crossing direction. 'falsified' shuffles WITHIDS with WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Across means from side to side, which is the same as measured along the width.

clue.text: Try-ons unexpectedly involving female?

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the next piece goes inside
unexpectedly means in a surprising way, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman unexpectedly tries on men's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of TRYONS takes in F. The whole clue is also the definition: a woman trying these on would be unexpected.
explanation.definitionFit: These are men's briefs with a Y-shaped front seam, an unexpected thing for a woman to try on.

clue.text: Working on an unforced error, City hit it here?

indicators.note: working means the letters are being worked over, kneaded into a new order

parts.words: on an unforced error, City hit it

explanation.surface: A football commentator says a City player, working on a careless mistake, struck the ball from this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is football, with City as a club; the answer is cricket. The anagram uses every letter of 'on an unforced error, City hit it'. It is the area just outside off stump where a batter cannot tell whether to play or leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue asks where the shot was played, and the answer names that place on a cricket pitch, so 'here' stands for it.

clue.text: Drought location ruined barbie, so Spooner phoned to say?

indicators.note: Dr Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, and saying it down the phone means the result is judged by sound

parts.note: something bust is broken or ruined
a Barbie is a doll

explanation.surface: Drought has spoiled the barbecue, which a man calls in to report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barbie' wants to be an Australian barbecue; it is the doll. Swapping the starts of BUST DOLL gives DUST BOLL, which sounds like the answer's second word.
explanation.definitionFit: A region whose soil has turned to blown dust after long drought, like the 1930s American prairies, is called this.

clue.text: See 1
Gathering in lobby, angry historians question 9 25

indicators.note: the shuffled letters gather the other piece in, enclosing it
angry letters are stirred up, so these are rearranged

parts.note: a hall is an entrance lobby

explanation.surface: Cross historians collect in a lobby to raise a question.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 25 is cricket's corridor of uncertainty, where the batter cannot decide whether to play at the ball or leave it.
explanation.definitionFit: A batter facing a ball in that awkward line agonises over whether to play a shot, the very dilemma this phrase voices.

clue.text: Inspiring science graduate can habitually take hash

indicators.note: inspiring means breathing in, so one piece takes the other inside

parts.note: can is slang for a toilet, a loo
BSc is a Bachelor of Science
to use a drug is to take it habitually

explanation.surface: A science graduate may habitually smoke hash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hash' looks like the drug; it is a stew. A loo is a British toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor's stew of meat and vegetables, the origin of Liverpool's scouse, which is a kind of hash.

clue.text: Extremely silly Slimefest brought to premature end

indicators.note: the piece is cut off before its natural finish, losing its last letter

parts.note: slime is goo and a fest is a fiesta, so a slime party is a goo fiesta

explanation.surface: A messy slime-themed festival was the silliest event, so it was shut down early.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Slimefest' as slime (GOO) plus fest (FIESTA), then cut the final A.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of goofy, meaning foolish or daft, so it means silliest of all.

clue.text: Common example of e.g. Liszt's output, being piano virtuoso

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a composer's work, as Liszt's
ens is the philosophical term for being or existence
P is short for piano, soft in music
an ace is an expert, a virtuoso

explanation.surface: Liszt's piano music typifies the work of a virtuoso.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common' looks like an adjective; it is a village common, one kind of this.
explanation.definitionFit: A common, a grassy public area, is a typical example of undeveloped land left free for public use.

clue.text: Where could you study hard while absorbing historic European capital?

indicators.note: one piece absorbs the other, taking it inside itself

parts.note: sore and hard both describe something painful or harsh to bear
Bonn was the capital of West Germany until reunification

explanation.surface: A question about a place for intense study while taking in a former capital's history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard' looks like an adverb with 'study'; it is SORE, which takes in BONN.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the famous university in Paris, a place where a student might study.

clue.text: Have uprising in prison, one result of playing 9 25?

parts.note: to own something is to have it

indicators.note: in a down entry, uprising means a letter moves higher, earlier in the word

parts.note: gaol is the British spelling of jail

explanation.surface: Inmates stage a prison riot, one result of a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uprising' moves the O of GAOL up a place. In the corridor, a defender hesitating over a ball can put it into their own net.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, the corridor of uncertainty is the gap between keeper and defenders where crosses often lead to scoring against your own side.

clue.text: Prepared cycles — and look at my profile when I'm on one!

definitions.text: look at my profile when I'm on one

indicators.note: cycles means the letters go round, so the last is brought to the front

parts.note: fruit that got ripe was made ready, prepared to eat

explanation.surface: A cyclist preparing a ride asks to be admired online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycles' moves the final E of GOTRIPE to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing off your own image is self-indulgent vanity, the kind of self-glorifying outing that boosts one's ego.

clue.text: People looking to take this in tower will be 1?

definitions.text: People looking to take this in tower will be 1?

parts.words: People looking to take this in tower will be 1?
parts.note: a pun on the Paris landmark's name, which sounds like a good long look; visitors there take in such a view and are caught by it, 1 being CAUGHT

explanation.surface: Sightseers at a tower hoping to see the view may get caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the Paris tower's name: it sounds just like the answer. Tourists who go up it to take in a good look will be 1 Across's first word, caught.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, full look at something striking is what sightseers want to take in.

clue.text: Say where A-T or Z-V are leading the solver's decision!

indicators.note: say means spoken aloud, so the phrase is taken by its sound

parts.words: where A-T or Z-V are leading
parts.note: both runs of the alphabet lead to the letter U, forwards from A through T or backwards from Z to V

explanation.surface: A setter teases the solver over which letters to use.
explanation.walkthrough: A to T leads up to U going forwards; Z to V does too going backwards. 'up to U' said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a choice is up to you means it is your decision, here the solver's.

clue.text: M. Fleetwood's bandmate gets edgy playing 9 25?

definitions.meaning: Mick Fleetwood's Fleetwood Mac bandmate was Stevie Nicks
to snick is to edge the ball in cricket, a likely outcome in that corridor

explanation.surface: A rock drummer's bandmate grows nervous on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edgy' looks like nervous; in cricket, edging the ball is called snicking it.
explanation.definitionFit: A snick is a fine edge off the bat, and a singer named Stevie Nicks shared a band with Mick Fleetwood.

clue.text: Dry sparkling white? Not in favour

indicators.note: not means excluding, so these letters are dropped

parts.note: prosecco is a sparkling white wine from Italy
pro means for, in favour of

explanation.surface: Someone rejects dry fizz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like a description of the wine; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Secco is the Italian wine term for dry, unsweetened.

clue.text: See 12
It may trim a beard — or a raw nerve!

indicators.note: trim does double duty: trimming the edges off these words leaves the inner run of letters

explanation.surface: A barber may trim a beard, or touch a raw nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beard' is a barley awn, not facial hair. 'trim' serves twice: trim the outer letters from 'a raw nerve'.
explanation.definitionFit: The awns are the bristly beards on barley; a machine that removes them is named for that job.

clue.text: See 9
15 ducks blocking mountain pass

indicators.note: the pieces sit inside and block the mountain, placed within it

parts.note: an Alp is a mountain
15 Down is OPEN SPACE, and a ley is an open grassy field
O is a duck, a zero score in cricket, so ducks gives two Os

explanation.surface: Birds in a meadow stop a mountain pass being crossed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pass' looks like a mountain route; it is a basketball pass lobbed for a teammate to dunk.
explanation.definitionFit: In basketball this is a high lob caught by a leaping teammate who scores in mid-air.

clue.text: Noble robes of ermine, perhaps, but right denied for wigging

indicators.note: the noble robes the other piece, wrapping it inside

parts.note: an earl is a noble

indicators.note: denied means refused, so this letter is taken away

parts.note: ermine is an example of a fur

explanation.surface: A peer's ermine-trimmed robes, but without his right to them, for a scolding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wigging' suggests a judge's wig; it is British slang for a telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: A wigging is a scolding, and getting a long angry talking-to is getting an earful.
